items.title: Ask Ethan: Can we solve the mysteries of the largest black holes?
items.summary: Out there in the Universe, there are some incredibly impressive astrophysical entities, including behemoths that dwarf anything we’re familiar with. There are stars hundreds of times more massive, and millions of times as luminous, as our own Sun is. There are galaxies and galaxy clusters thousands of times as massive as our Milky Way and Local Group. And there are black holes out there that not only dwarf our own Sun, but black holes that are so massive, they’re comparable in mass to all of the stars in the Milky Way galaxy combined. Some of them, quite puzzlingly, at first glance, even exist extremely early on in cosmic history: just a few billion years after the hot Big Bang first began. At those extremes, the largest black holes pose a number of important cosmic questions. How did they grow so big so fast? Can physics even account for the highest-mass ones? And why do we see the biggest ones at such great distances, rather than close by? Is there something missing in our understanding? These questions, among others, inspired Eric Trant to write in and ask about TON 618 : the black hole that first challenged our conventional understanding of how these supermassive black holes form and grow up in our Universe. “My question tonight has to do with TON 618, the largest black hole we’ve observed to date, at ~66 billion solar masses. Seeing as we’re incredibly far away, observing it as it was 10.8 billion years ago… how did it grow to be so large when it’s only [been] 3 billion years [since] the universe itself [began]? It also seems odd that we don’t see more of similar size, closer to home?” The supermassive black holes that we know of pose many mysteries, and TON 618 is the one that kicked off our current series of questions. Here’s the story of how we got to where we are today. This set of illustrations explains how a large black hole can form from the direct collapse of a massive cloud of gas within a couple of hundred million years after the Big Bang. Streams of gas, if they’re sufficiently cold, can lead to the direct collapse of a “seed” black hole of several tens of thousands (at least) of solar masses, which can form even prior to any stars forming in the surrounding young galaxy. As the galaxy and black hole grow, eventually the stellar mass content will outweigh the more slowly-growing black hole. Dark matter, which can’t become “cold” by shedding heat in the same way, can’t form a black hole similarly. Credit : NASA/STScI/Leah Hustak Back in the 20th century, black holes were much more of a theoretical prediction than they were an observational puzzle. Although the idea of a black hole dates all the way back to the 18th century — originating with the predictions of John Michell from Newtonian considerations — they came into the mainstream with Karl Schwarzschild’s exact solution to Einstein’s general relativity in 1916. Schwarzschild showed that if you start with a distribution of matter at rest in general relativity and you just release those masses and let them gravitate, they’ll collapse to form a non-rotating black hole of a given mass, with an event horizon at a particular distance, R , known as the Schwarzschild radius . Any mass that crosses over the event horizon adds to the mass of the black hole, and early theoretical work was able to calculate the maximum rate at which black holes could grow by accreting matter. From the core-collapse of massive stars, which occur in supernova events, initial black holes could be formed. And then, over time, these “seed” black holes would gain mass, grow by accretions and mergers, and would sink to the centers of galaxies. There, they could reside as supermassive black holes. Both the stellar mass black holes (from dying, massive stars) and supermassive black holes (at the centers of massive galaxies) would then be expected to exist. Discovered in 1964 as an X-ray emitting source consistent with a stellar object orbiting a black hole, Cygnus X-1 represents the first black hole candidate known within the Milky Way. Cygnus X-1 is located near large active regions of star formation in the Milky Way: precisely the location expected to find an X-ray emitting black hole binary. Credit : X-ray: NASA/CXC; Optical: Digitized Sky Survey It wasn’t until the 1950s and 1960s, however, that we began to detect objects that served as candidate black holes. Initially, the observations that suggested black holes physically existed came far away, in terms of wavelength, from the light we’re used to seeing: X-ray light and radio light. In the X-ray, the very bright source known as Cygnus X-1 was discovered in 1964, during a rocket flight. When black holes have another star orbiting them, particularly if it’s a very massive star, the extremely dense black hole can siphon mass off of its companion, producing a system known as an X-ray binary , where the black hole emits X-rays from the heated, accelerated matter that accumulates around it. Until the development of gravitational wave astronomy , this was the main method for detecting stellar mass black holes. On the other end of both the electromagnetic and mass spectrums, far into the radio and corresponding to incredibly large masses, quasars began to be observed. Originally standing for QUAsi-StellAr Radio Sources (QSRS, or quasars), these objects are now known to be located at the centers of galaxies , even though, back when they were first discovered, the host galaxy itself was normally too faint to be seen. Now, we know these to be active, supermassive black holes, surrounded by accretion disks and emitting powerful jets of matter that can extend for millions or even tens of millions of light-years in length. This illustration of a radio-loud quasar that is embedded within a star-forming galaxy gives a close-up look of how giant radio galaxies are expected to emerge. At the center of an active galaxy with a supermassive black hole, jets are emitted that slam into the larger galactic halo, energizing the gas and plasma and causing radio emissions in the form of jets close by the black hole, and then plumes and/or lobes farther away. Both supermassive and stellar-mass black holes have overwhelming evidence supporting their existence, but supermassive black holes may heat matter to the highest temperatures of all, accelerating particles to even beyond the GZK cutoff set by particle physics. Credit : ESA/C. Carreau This was the standard picture at the turn of the century: we had a theoretical maximum limit for how big black holes could get, we knew of stellar mass black holes and had a theory of how they formed (from core-collapse supernovae), and we knew about supermassive black holes at the centers of galaxies, including some very active ones like active galactic nuclei and quasars, normally located very far away. Sure, nearby, we also had the occasional active galaxy, but since the Universe was denser, experienced more major mergers between galaxies, and formed stars more rapidly in the distant past, it made sense that these quasars would tend to be more likely to be seen early on in cosmic history. Today, we assumed, the black holes are still there, but they’re more difficult to observe, since they don’t emit those same high levels of radiation that they do in the aftermath of events like major galactic mergers or intense star-formation events. Today’s galaxies are mostly quiet places, but the occasional active galaxy that we do see nearby often has both substantial X-ray and radio emissions, and supermassive black holes can often be inferred by the presence of their jets. items.title: 4 hilarious ancient Greek comedies — that still hold up today
items.summary: Comedy is a strange genre. Even the best comedies are strongly tied to the time and place of their composition. Just try getting all the jokes in Shakespeare without peeking at the footnotes for help. But every now and again, a comedic gem shines through the ages, even from as far back as Classical Greece. Maybe this is because ancient Greek ideas are so deeply embedded in Western culture, or maybe Athens just produced some truly brilliant playwrights. Whatever the case, some Greek comedies still entertain millennia after their first performances. Ancient Greek comedy encompasses centuries, so scholars often break it down into three distinct periods . Old Comedy (5th century BC) is characterized by its focus on social and political issues, with plenty of farce and innuendo. Middle Comedy (400–320 BC) moves away from the political to favor myth-based parodies and stock characters. Finally, New Comedy (320 to the mid-3rd century) leans into a style modern audiences would see as similar to situational comedy, while also introducing the five-act structure that would come to dominate European theater. Today, we look at four Greek plays: three Old Comedies and one New Comedy. This split isn’t because Old Comedies are more amusing than those from the other periods. It is, in part, because the Middle Comedies are mostly lost to us, and few New Comedies have survived to the present day. Even among the relatively better-represented Old Comedies, all the works we have today were penned by the playwright Aristophanes. It’s a sad thought, but many hilarious and innovative works may be lost to time. Thankfully, we can still enjoy these plays. A scene from a 1947 production of Aristophanes’ Lysistrata at Oslo’s Centralteatret. ( Credit : A.S. Polyfoto / Wikimedia Commons) Lysistrata (411 BC) O women, if we would compel the men to bow to Peace, … We must refrain from every depth of love …. Why do you turn your backs? Where are you going? Why do you bite your lips and shake your heads? Why are your faces blanched? Why do you weep? Aristophanes’ best-known play, Lysistrata , is an anti-war farce that puts most other comedies written in the last 2,000 years to shame. Performed during the Peloponnesian War, the play is at once incredibly raunchy, remarkably clever, horribly dated, and effortlessly timeless. It opens with Lysistrata calling a meeting of women from the warring Greek city-states. As the war drags on and men are dying on far-off battlefields, families at home are being broken. Despite women having no voice in government, Lysistrata proposes a radical plan to force the men to the negotiating table: a sex strike across the whole of Greece. Although she struggles to get the others to agree, the strike begins. The Greek women lock themselves in the Acropolis, both to keep their distance from the men and to hold the Athenian treasury hostage. The strike lasts a while despite various attempts by the increasingly desperate men to get the women to come to terms. Meanwhile, Lysistrata must keep the women motivated by reminding them how important their work is (and how giving up too soon will prevent women in future plays from receiving good roles). Eventually, the Greek men relent and negotiate an end to the war. There is much, let’s say, celebration. Lysistrata is a farce, obviously, and one that holds up better than others in some ways. For instance, the ancient Greeks would have found the idea of women taking such direct political action absurd, and the plot relies on gender stereotypes that would have made more sense in the extremely sexist Athenian society. That said, the play inverts those stereotypes, too, and today it can be read as an anti-war comedy with a feminist edge. The fact that misguided quagmires seem to never go out of fashion doesn’t hurt its popularity. The play continues to enjoy new translations and adaptations to this day. In 2015, Spike Lee adapted it into a film titled Chi-Raq , moving the action from the Mediterranean to Chicago’s South Side. Dyskolos (316 BC) This man has lived here a reasonably long time and has gladly talked in his life to no one, has spoken first to no one except — of necessity, since he is a neighbor and passes by — me, Pan. And he immediately regrets it, I’m sure. Written by the poet Menander, Dyskolos is the only New Comedy play to have survived in a nearly complete form; all others are missing large segments of their text. It covers themes immediately recognizable to modern audiences through its romantic-comedy elements. The play begins with Pan, the Satyr-shaped god of nature, describing one of his neighbors, the reclusive, misanthropic Knemon. Pan explains that Knemon has a pious daughter whom he will reward by making a rich city boy, Sostratos, fall in love with her. Additionally, Pan wants Knemon to have something of a redemption arc, even if against his will. As arranged by Pan, Sostratos sends one of his servants to speak with Knemon about his daughter. Sostratos initially has high hopes for the meeting, but the servant, Pyrrhias, returns beaten nearly senseless by Knemon, who hates visitors. Sostratos is advised to try working in the fields next to Knemon’s as a way of earning his favor — after all, grouchy poor farmers are more likely to favor marrying their daughters to other farmers. At the same time, Sostratos’ family heads off to make a sacrifice to Pan after dreaming a terrible omen: Their son doing manual labor. Hijinks ensue. Knemon falls into a well and is rescued by other members of the cast. While recuperating, he resolves to be friendlier — since being a jerk got him stuck at the bottom of a well — and gives an extremely sunburnt Sostaratos his blessing to marry his daughter. In the end, several people get married, and everyone lives happily ever after. Between each of the five acts, a chorus of drunken Pan worshippers dance to music. Interestingly, they don’t exit the stage after their performance and lounge about the stage even when they’re not needed. The play is very class-conscious for its time. It features considerable intermingling up and down the social hierarchy. While it offers an idealized view of marriage, especially among members of different classes, none of the characters are presented as perfect or better than others because of their status or birth. An illustration depicting a scene from Aristophanes’ The Clouds . It shows Strepsiades and Pheidippides having a discussion while Socrates hangs out in a basket. ( Credit : Wikimedia Commons) The Clouds (423 BC) Consider, therefore, how you have trumpeted from a little belly so small; and how is it not probable that this air, being boundless, should thunder so loudly? The play Plato blamed for Socrates’ death, Aristophanes’ The Clouds is a hysterical send-up of faux-intellectualism and those who want to weaponize it. The play presents a version of Socrates very different from Plato’s, resembling more a pre-Socratic philosopher or even a sophist. The results are enduringly funny, even if it didn’t help Socrates’ case. Its story begins with the middle-aged Strepsiades in a jam. His wife has encouraged their son, Pheidippides, to live like an Ancient Greek NEET. Despite being an adult, he bums around at home, wastes his family’s money betting on the ponies, and refuses to contribute. As you might expect, this causes the debts to start piling up. Luckily, Strepsiades has a solution. The Thinkery, a school for those who want to learn to turn bad arguments into winning ones, is taking new students. Strepsiades hopes to enroll his son so he can weasel the family out of debt, but he is forced to attend himself when his son refuses to become a nerd. Freshly matriculated as a non-traditional student, Strepsiades meets the great and famous headmaster, Socrates. items.title: Mapped: Every known (and suspected) road in the Roman Empire
items.summary: Rome wasn’t built in a day . All roads lead to Rome . A recent study now links those two well-worn proverbs by suggesting that the footprint of Roman road infrastructure was 59% larger than previously thought. The revelation isn’t just quantitative — a network with a finer mesh might change what we think life was like across Rome’s vast domain. From Hadrian’s Wall to the Persian Gulf The findings come from the research team behind Itiner-e, a project that published a digital atlas of the Empire in Nature’s Scientific Data in late 2025. They mapped about 186,000 miles (just under 300,000 km) of roads across Rome at its greatest extent. This was in the 2nd century AD, when the Empire sprawled from Hadrian’s Wall in northern England to the western shores of the Persian Gulf. The previous reference catalog, the Digital Atlas of Roman and Medieval Civilizations (DARMC, now known as Mapping Past Societies), tallied around 117,100 miles (188,500 km) — meaning the new figure is 59% longer than the earlier total. Roman roads transported more than people and goods, they also moved ideas and religions to faraway places, as shown by this altar to the Persian god Mithras, discovered in 2010 in Scotland, at the very northern edge of Rome’s road network. ( Credit : National Museums Scotland) To be clear, the researchers have not discovered that Rome had a secret “lost” highway system. They didn’t discover a massive imperial ring road or dig up a legionary engineering project concealed for two millennia. The explanation is less Indiana Jones, more Beancounter Bob. Earlier compilations of the Roman road network tended to privilege great, well-documented routes like the Via Appia (Rome to Brindisi) or the Via Egnatia (from Albania’s coast to Byzantium). The connective tissue between those major roads — the first- and last-mile bits that actually got produce to market, villagers to town, soldiers to frontiers, and tax collectors to your door — received less attention. What the Itiner-e researchers did was create, from a wide and scattered body of evidence, a much fuller and more precise record of roads that definitely existed, and also ones that researchers suspect existed, with varying degrees of confidence. Itiner-e’s final result makes the imbalance plain. Of its roughly 186,000 miles of roads, only about 34.6% are classified as main arteries. The remaining two-thirds are secondary routes or smaller. Roman roads were much like ours: a mixture of grand highways, regional roads, and rural lanes. While the major thoroughfares get all the press, the smaller ones probably played an important part in everyday work. Cold War spy satellite photos, repurposed As an international project with contributors from the universities of Barcelona and Aarhus, among others, Itiner-e built its Roman road atlas (the expanded version) in three painstaking phases. First, they drew on literary sources, inscriptions, gazetteers, excavation reports, and earlier atlases to identify where the roads should be. Then, they used satellite imagery, aerial photography, and topographic maps to determine where those roads did plausibly run. And finally, they digitized the whole thing, segment by segment, into a geographic information system. A sample of DARMC road mapping in southern Britannia and northern Gaul (now the southern UK and northern France, plus the Low Countries, respectively). Note how the course of Roman roads still corresponds to present-day centers of night-time luminescence (e.g. the roads converging on London). The more extensive road network formulated by Itiner-e may not only teach us more about how ancient Rome worked, but also how its infrastructure has influenced the societies that came after the Empire and continues to affect the present. ( Credit : Mapping Past Societies/Harvard University) Among the images the researchers used were Cold War-era spy satellite photographs — now used to spot infrastructure much older than the type that intelligence agencies were looking for in the 20th century. Even centuries after their disappearance at, well, street level, Roman roads can still be identified from above as subtle marks in fields, slight differences in vegetation, and subtle traces in the terrain. The resulting atlas is not, however, a definitive catalog. Its most salient feature may be that it evaluates how confirmed or contested each mapped route actually is. In fact, only 2.7% of the total length is classed as certain , meaning there is a physical road surface left from Roman days. Nearly 90% is conjectured : inferred from a web of literary references, terrain logic, and pattern-matching. The remaining 7.4% is outright hypothetical . The latter two categories are not an admission of failure. They visualize a problem that most Roman road maps all too easily conceal: a clean line on paper (or screen) can look much more definitive than the evidence behind it. Or to be blunt: They’re often scholarly best guesses dressed up as solid roads. To let the evidence, current and future, have the last word, Itiner-e attached source information and confidence assessments to each road segment. Later researchers can then continue the fight over which highways and byways need to be refined, challenged, or scrapped altogether from the map. Itiner-e wears this uncertainty as a badge, not a blemish. The idea is that in historical research, a frank and open assessment of uncertainty will lead to a higher form of precision. That key principle of the scientific method is ignored all too often, and not just in Roman studies. The oldest evidence of the Roman road network This modern, layered, conditional map is the digital descendant of the Tabula Peutingeriana . Itiner-e’s strange and magnificent ancestor is the oldest cartographic evidence we have of the Roman road network. But not quite as old as Rome itself: the Tabula is a copy on medieval parchment of a map tradition that harkens back to the time of Augustus. That copy, dating from the 12th century and now at Austria’s National Library in Vienna, thus only provides indirect evidence of how the Romans themselves mapped their roads. Two examples of how Itiner-e has increased our understanding of the extent of the Roman road network: adding a lot of mileage in some areas, such as northern France (top), and considerably less in others, such as southern Turkey (bottom). ( Credit : Itiner-e: A high-resolution dataset of roads of the Roman Empire, in Nature) Measuring 6.75 meters by 34 centimeters — the dimensions of an unwieldy scarf — the Tabula is not a map in the classical sense (pun intended) but rather a route diagram. It compresses the north-south dimension, stretches coastlines, and rearranges geography to make routes and distances legible. The Tabula depicts more than 550 cities and 3,500 other place names, along with the way stations and distances that separate them. It covers the Empire itself, but stretches all the way to India, showing how the grasp of Rome’s geographic imagination exceeded its actual reach. One segment is missing, so Britain is not fully represented on the Tabula , which otherwise is a remarkably intact witness of Rome’s practical attitude towards mapcraft: no Here be dragons , or other mythical or religious infusions that distorted later maps. With its focus on connectivity rather than geographical accuracy, the Tabula weirdly prefigures the schematic and now-iconic map of the London Underground, designed by Harry Beck some 1,900 years later. Itiner-e draws on the Tabula and many other sources, but the contrast is revealing. Where the Tabula is visually eccentric, Itiner-e is digitally exacting. Both, however, show that mapping a road network is not just a matter of sticking to the main roads. It’s a matter of deciding what counts as a road, and that in the context of what the map wants us to understand. Roman roads may have been a military construct to start with; they eventually did mu

items.title: A Forgotten Fix for American Racial Strife
items.summary: In 1967, Marshall Lee was living in Philadelphia and becoming a Black revolutionary. “We were crazy, involved in a whole lot of stupid stuff,” Lee told me. “If it had not been for The Crisis ”—Harold Cruse’s The Crisis of the Negro Intellectual , published that same year—“I do not know what would have happened to me.” Lee thinks he might have ended up in prison, or dead. Instead, he became a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan, where he studied with Cruse—“somebody who helped to bring some clarity to Black revolutionary movements.” In the late 1960s and through the ’70s, The Crisis of the Negro Intellectual helped give shape to the aspiring Black revolutionary movement. It also became a cornerstone of the new discipline of Black studies; Henry Louis Gates Jr. was assigned the book in three different classes at Yale. Cruse’s work circulated so widely in part because it cut across truisms of radical movements and therefore made people angry: Audre Lorde described The Crisis as rife with “inaccuracies, misrepresentations and plain lies.” In the 2010s and early ’20s, young Black radicals were again talking about the intersection of class and race, criticizing the politics of respectability, and questioning whether white liberals would ever concede power. But few of them were talking about Cruse, whose polarizing qualities had helped consign him to obscurity. They should have been. The Crisis tells three stories at once: Cruse’s own story, the story of his generation of Black people in Harlem, and the story of Black America. All three narratives seem to culminate naturally in 1967, when militant Black nationalism was capturing the public imagination. Really, they’re all still culminating today. And Cruse, I think, might have helped explain why the Black struggle for progress—and broader American efforts toward equality—seem stuck in the same cycles that plagued the movement six decades ago. He might also have had some unwelcome suggestions for how to break out of them. Harold Cruse was born in Petersburg, Virginia, in 1916. His mother worked as a domestic servant, his father in a factory. Petersburg, which before the Civil War had been home to more free Black people than any other city in the South, was a bastion of Black institutions. Later, Cruse would use his 1987 book, Plural but Equal , to ask what might have happened if, instead of focusing political energy on integration, Black Americans had directed it toward providing their own communities with the same level of resources that white communities had. [ Read: ‘Race neutral’ is the new ‘separate but equal’ ] Cruse’s childhood was itinerant. Eventually, he and his father ended up in Harlem, where he became enthralled by the characters of the Harlem Renaissance. Countee Cullen taught at his junior high school, and as a young man, Cruse attended public lectures by Richard Wright, Claude McKay, and W. E. B. Du Bois. During World War II, Cruse joined the Army and spent time in Algeria—where the Arabs resisting the French felt an affinity with Black soldiers—and then Italy, where he was impressed by communism. The underground Algerian movement and the Italian underground partisans, he later wrote, were “ professionals not amateurs”—a distinction that he used to dismiss much of the American activism he encountered in decades to come. The characteristic that would make Cruse’s work exceptionally compelling would also block his path to public acclaim: His commitment to justice was mixed with a curiosity that defied doctrinaire thinking. In his first writing job, at the Communist Party paper the Daily Worker , he submitted articles that explored the complexity of Black life rather than simply celebrating heroes of the struggle for Black liberation. He was skeptical of integration and gravitated toward a circle of Black writers and artists who believed that they should first prioritize building a stronger sense of Black identity. He helped found the short-lived Harlem Writers Club, a collective of writers who felt a “need to break away from enforced interracialism”—a position that put him at odds with Communist leadership. Disillusioned, he critiqued the “cliquish remoteness” of a Black communist-aligned paper, Freedom , lambasting its writers as “intellectual prisoners of the dying left-wing movement.” Cruse knew that his resistance to norms that defined American conversations about race was risky: When he was working on The Crisis of the Negro Intellectual , he told friends, “If I publish it, I’m going to have to leave the country.” The Crisis insisted that although the United States imagines itself as a nation of individuals, it is really a collection of social, ethnic, and religious groups. The much-vaunted individual rights that the U.S. guarantees are actually secured by group power. White people as a group have more power, so white individuals have more rights. Within this framework, integration into white society will always mean subordination—and a few privileges for compliant Blacks. The extreme alternative is similarly unpromising: Cruse argued that Black leftists compensate for their marginalization within political organizations by becoming even more militant defenders of sectarian orthodoxies, further alienating them from the Black masses. The solution to this stalemate between ineffectual opposites was, he thought, for Black Americans as a group to seek cultural, political, and economic self-determination. Cruse argued that the Harlem Renaissance had marked a rare opportunity to build the sort of internally self-governing community that Petersburg had once been. But he believed that that movement had fallen short because, despite its artistic influence, it did not braid culture with politics and economics. White people owned the property and businesses that served Harlem residents, thereby appropriating the profit of those enterprises from Black communities. [ Read: The Harlem Renaissance was bigger than Harlem ] What the Black masses really wanted, Cruse thought, was not integration but rather resources that would meet their basic needs. The first political goal attached to Black group consciousness, then, ought to be to block white people from extracting resources that should serve Black people—with the second aim of Black communities building resilient community infrastructure, including cooperatively owned businesses and locally controlled third-party politics. The mid-1960s were a moment when those goals seemed like they might be achievable—if, Cruse warned, Black Americans could avoid falling prey to sectarianism and impatience. (“In the place of a matured social vision,” he wrote, “there will always be those who will gladly substitute the catastrophic and glorious act of martyrdom and self-immolation for a cause.”) On top of the dangers of rash action, Cruse feared that Black intellectuals, including leaders of the civil-rights movement, might be too interested in their own middle-class existence to genuinely encourage or arrange such radical change. Cruse’s ideas about communal self-determination may have faded in prominence in part because of his knack for making enemies: The Crisis targeted the most venerated and powerful figures in the Black community, including leaders of the integration movement, and they had no trouble finding platforms to denounce him. Cruse also criticized those on the left, both Black and white; even some people who were most ideologically aligned with him found the book’s ideas unpalatable. Importantly, Cruse also had a record of bigoted statements about groups including Black women, southern Blacks, West Indians, and Jews. The Crisis includes, among other much-scrutinized comments, claims of “nationalistic aggressiveness” by Jews. Cruse also routinely stereotyped Black women writers as motivated by “axe-grinding against black men.” [ Read: The America that killed George Floyd ] Or perhaps Cruse’s arguments were forgotten because his central message—t

items.title: Fixing Up Our Home Means Making Memories My Husband Might Lose
items.summary: Aphantasia: A Floor Plan by Josepha Natzke Front Stairwell The home’s previous owners painted the stairwell a dark mauve. You and I are close to the top step. The white beam of our bed frame looms between us, its length caught on the last corner. Since we have been married we have moved four times, and every time we move furniture together, we argue. I find myself warning you of this each time. Don’t you remember? This doesn’t go well, does it? We approach these tasks very differently. I plan, you move. I fret, you haul. We sweat and grunt at each other. The sharp edge of the bed frame digs in at the soft pink of the wall, exposing chalky plaster beneath. We argue angles. I think the gash on the wall is your fault. There is a clouded window watching us from above, its frame the color of a thorough bruise. Also above our heads, a framed painting that the previous owners, whose names we know from the closing documents are Maximeno and Ramona, left behind: a man and a woman, dancing together. A clock looms in the painting next to them, an indeterminate reminder about time. Lot Characteristics and Size We bought this house because it was one of the only places in this northwest Chicago neighborhood that we could afford, and because we knew how to do the work it needed. Together we have learned how to rewire outlets, frame walls, mend drywall. Between us is a love for fixing and patching, and because of this we have always lived in houses that are in the throes of entropy. We try our best to care for them as we put them back together. I can easily envision the many settings of my childhood: the blackberry patch by my childhood home, the cluttered corners of my bedroom. This home sits on a lot 25 feet wide and 125 feet long on a narrow city street lined mostly with cars and litter. It was built in 1895 and looks small in comparison to the buildings on either side. On its front is a second-floor balcony unlike any we have seen in our years living in the city: a mildewed porch lined with a white railing. It sags in the middle and likely isn’t up to code. The day we close, we drag two camp chairs onto it to bask in the sun and share a lukewarm bottle of prosecco. Bathroom When we move in, I arm myself with sponges and sprays. I start from the bathroom ceiling and work my way down the walls, mirrors, and tiling to the floor. I remove layers of debris from the past lives lived here. There are rings of brown grease on the ceiling. I pull hair and toenails softened by water from the shower drain. There is a bottle of soap and an industrial roll of single-ply toilet paper under the sink. I gag as I wipe down the scummy corners of the shower. Despite my body’s physical reaction, though, I don’t mind too much. The drips of soap and strands of gray hair are the natural castoffs of the body. A bathroom is where you go to remove these things. It’s disgusting, but it’s also intimate. In the 30 years that Maximeno and Ramona owned this house, they took some decorative liberties. Not only are the walls of each room painted bright colors, but this home is a time-traveling funhouse: Many things are not what they seem. The towel rack in the bathroom is actually a curtain rod with spiny finials. Here, as in other rooms, the gaps between the window and its frame are sealed with clear tape. There are hooks in the back of the door which, when I lean forward with my rag to wipe them down, are actually just nails covered in drippy coats of paint. Living Room Your father has been sending us scans of his childhood photos. He sends them in alarming spurts, belying a nostalgia he never shows face-to-face. There is a photograph of you and your younger sister Cornelia on a back deck, or maybe a restaurant patio. Your curls swell in the humidity. Your arm is thrown around Cornelia’s shoulder: a happy older brother. “Where was this taken?” I ask. You examine the photo for a moment and shrug. “No clue.” Another: You’re older, maybe 16, sitting on the ground outside. Almost every inch of your skin is covered in red mud, which has dried in the Alabama sun. I look over at you on the couch and laugh until you blush. “What the hell were you doing?” But you have no memory of the patio, the mud, or any part of the other photos your father sends. You have never been able to recall specific memories from your childhood. Even now, in your early 30s, you forget small things that most of us remember: friends’ last names, birthdays, bars we’ve visited before. We’ve debated whether this was caused by the trauma of your parents’ divorce when you were 10, or from something else from your childhood, which you spent being ferried back and forth between them across state lines. There’s a possibility that the memory loss stems from trauma, some assault which your mind then chose to forget. I can easily envision the many settings of my childhood: the blackberry patch by my childhood home, the cluttered corners of my bedroom. My past is an associative landscape, a carpet rolled out before me asking to be remembered. But these kinds of scenes in your past elude you. Your eyes flicker over these photos without recognizing them, learning their details for the first time. Maximeno and Ramona painted the living room pink. Bright, pepto bismol, lacquered lip gloss, watermelon candy, texture like a drug store lipstick. A throbbing and crawling color so saturated that I’m convinced when we get up from the couch to walk to another room we must be seeing everything through a haze of green, the color on the other end of the spectrum of the red tones, like in middle school where the teacher had us all stare at a red apple for thirty seconds—I ask you, do you remember? —and when we looked at a white space on the wall afterwards, there was an apple’s silhouette, green, seared into our vision. You have no idea what I’m talking about. You don’t remember learning this in middle school, or anywhere else. And to be fair, maybe that’s just because no one ever taught you. Sometimes your father sends the photos in a group text with Cornelia. Others he shares only with you in an email with no subject line. Once or twice, he sends them only to me. Young versions of you, smiling wide; cheerful emissaries from your forgotten past. Kitchen (Eat-in) We will have to demolish most of this house to restore it, and so we should know better than to become attached to these bright walls and strange finishes. This dreamsicle palace that Maximeno and Ramona created is only our temporary home. But its delirium casts a spell over us. The kitchen is painted three shades of yellow: mustard, marigold, ochre. There is also a stenciled brick pattern behind the oven. There are also white floor-to-ceiling stripes on either side of the wall heater. There are handmade cabinets with glass fronts—but no! You tap them and it’s only a dull click with your nail. Plexiglass. This home is a facade in yelling color. Every interaction with it yields some inexplicable and precarious wonder. The day we move in, the kitchen sink doesn’t let out any water. We wonder, panicked, if the city turned off our service. Down we go to the strip of grass between the sidewalk in front of the house and the street. We pry off the plastic cover and peer down at the shutoff valve. We try several tools to see if we can turn it one way or another. This is illegal, of course. They don’t work, because the city uses some special wrench with a proprietary number of angles to prevent exactly what we’re doing. I go back inside, stare at the sink, and unscrew the nozzle of the faucet. I remove the filter and detach the pull-down handle, and then I discover that the top of the tube is filled with tiny smooth rocks which have blocked the water flow. Once I empty them and reassemble the faucet, the water flows just fine. On the door of the cupboard above the oven, where I decide to put baking supplies, there are countless phone numbers scrawled in pencil. There are printed pages of more phone n

items.title: Exclusive Cover Reveal of BIOLAMP by Dennis James Sweeney
items.summary: Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the cover of Biolamp by Dennis James Sweeney, which will be published on April 20, 2027 by Autumn House Press. You can pre-order your copy here . In Biolamp , Dennis James Sweeney confronts ecological collapse, technological alienation, and the lingering weight of history with startling imagination and unexpected hope. In their sophomore collection, Sweeney’s poems inhabit a world shaped by loss and transformation, where decay becomes a source of energy, and the past remains visible in the landscapes of the present. Through dreamlike imagery and inventive language, Sweeney explores what it means to feel deeply in an era defined by environmental crisis and digital disconnection. The collection suggests that feeling itself—even dread, grief, or uncertainty—is evidence of life and a reason to continue imagining new futures. Here’s the cover, designed by Mike Corrao, with art by Connor “Phib” Dainty: Dennis James Sweeney: I first encountered Connor “Phib” Dainty’s collages back when Twitter was real. His collages take old-school images of nature and remix them into surreal landscapes with people passing through, and they always felt kindred with the moods of my writing. I had originally asked my editor, Christine Stroud of Autumn House Press, if we could use an image of a rainbow monolith being photographed by a tiny black and white man. Christine reached out to Phib to see if he’d be open to us using one of his pieces for the cover, and (yay!) he was. Once we had the go-ahead, Christine had some other great suggestions of collages from Phib’s catalog, which better fit the surreal environmental landscapes of Biolamp . Designer Mike Corrao did mock-ups with several of our suggestions, and they were all beautiful. To my surprise, the one that felt like it had to be the cover used an image I hadn’t been magnetized to at first, but that I now love for the book. The moment taught me that an image on its own is very different than the context of an image on a book cover. Corrao’s design, paired with Phib’s collage, perfectly captured the dark blossom of the book, the way its stalks are both ghostly and life-filled. And just over the horizon, I imagine, is the ocean that plays a significant role in many of the book’s poems: a sea of overwhelmingness and relief, just out of sight. This process also reminded me of the collaborative nature of being a writer, which I’ve been thinking about ever since writing How to Submit . The conversations around the text are the text, in a certain way, and they reveal things about what I’ve written that I never would otherwise have known. Biolamp’s cover revealed to me a hunger that underlies these poems’ lushness. It reminds me who I was (the man crawling through the sand) and who I am now (among the flowers, beyond the horizon’s edge). Mike Corrao: Designing the cover for Biolamp was a very fun challenge. The author requested we use the work of talented Minnesota-based collage artist, Connor “Phib” Dainty. And I can see why. Dainty’s work hits the mark spot-on with its tension between the earthly flora and lunar tundra. There’s a soft uncanniness to the nature depicted. And the central pull of that lone figure, standing before this surreal forest. It all felt a perfect match for Sweeney’s poetry. The primary challenge in this design was to explore how we could integrate text into pre-existing art (a design challenge as old as time). This piece is particularly generous due to the negative space at the top and bottom of the composition, which presents a natural lead for the cover’s composition. Pulling in some nice speckled papery textures, weaving the text through the pale foliage, I wanted to introduce the typography as another part of the collage. Text integrated into the uncanny nature of the artwork—how Sweeney’s poetry itself searches to connect what’s natural to what’s written. This cover was a pleasure to put together.
